card.title: Yksi kirjain, yksi ääni
body: Finnish is spelled the way it is said. Every letter is pronounced, and always the same way.
Most letters sound the way you would guess. Four need attention: ä, ö, y and j.

examples.en: night · ö like the i in “bird”
one · y like German ü: “ee” with rounded lips
yeah · j like the y in “yes”

steps.title: Kuuntele · Listen and pick the spelling
steps.note: ä is the a in “cat”. a is the a in “father”.

steps.title: Kuuntele · Listen and pick the spelling
steps.note: yö means night. jo (already) is a different word.

steps.title: Kuuntele · Listen and pick the spelling
steps.note: j always sounds like the y in “yes”. juna is a train.

steps.title: Kuuntele · Listen and pick the spelling
steps.note: y is not i and not u: say “ee” and round your lips. kyllä means yes.

steps.title: Paino · Stress
steps.note: Always on the first syllable, in every Finnish word.

card.title: Pitkä vai lyhyt?
body: A double letter is a long sound, and length changes the meaning.
Hold a double vowel for twice as long. Before a double consonant, make a tiny pause.

card.title: Kaksi joukkuetta
body: Finnish vowels come in two teams. Back: a, o, u. Front: ä, ö, y.
One word uses one team, never both. e and i are neutral and can go with either; a word with only e and i takes the front team.
Endings follow the word: talo → talossa, but metsä → metsässä. What these endings mean comes later. For now, hear how they match.

examples.en: a town in Lapland · only e and i, so front

steps.title: Kumpi joukkue? · Which team?
steps.sub: Which team of vowels does this word use?
steps.note: talo has a and o: back team.

steps.title: Kumpi joukkue? · Which team?
steps.sub: Which team of vowels does this word use?
steps.note: kylä (village) has y and ä: front team.

steps.title: Kumpi joukkue? · Which team?
steps.sub: Which team of vowels does this word use?
steps.note: kahvi has a, so it is back team. The i is neutral.

steps.title: Kumpi joukkue? · Which team?
steps.sub: Which team of vowels does this word use?
steps.note: Only e and i, so front: Helsingissä.

steps.title: Kumpi pääte? · Which ending fits?
steps.note: metsä has ä, so the ending has ä: metsässä.

card.title: Ei a:ta eikä the:tä
body: Finnish has no words for “a” or “the”. The context tells you which one is meant.

examples.en: coffee, a coffee or the coffee
bus, a bus or the bus

steps.title: Mitä se tarkoittaa? · What can it mean?
choices: coffee, a coffee or the coffee
steps.answer: coffee, a coffee or the coffee

card.title: Hän = he tai she
card.titleEn: One word for he and she
body: There is no grammatical gender. hän means he and she.
In everyday speech people say se for both, and for “it”.

examples.en: it, and he or she in speech

steps.title: Valitse · Pick one
steps.sub: How do you say “she” in Finnish?
steps.note: hän is both he and she.

card.title: Pääte kertoo, kuka
body: The end of a verb shows who is doing it, so the pronoun is often left out: Olen Sofia means “I am Sofia”.
There is no future tense either. The present covers it.

steps.title: Kuka puhuu? · Who is it about?
steps.sub: The -n at the end of olen means…

card.title: Pienet sanat ovat päätteitä
body: English uses small words: in, from, to. Finnish glues an ending onto the word instead.
You will meet them one at a time, each with a card like this one, before any sentence uses them.

blocks.text: Finnish is written almost exactly as it sounds: every letter is pronounced, always the same way.
Stress is always on the first syllable of a word: HUO-men-ta, NÄ-ke-miin.

head: Letter
Sounds like
rows: German ü — say 'ee' with rounded lips

blocks.text: Double letters are long, and length changes the meaning:
Exaggerate long sounds at first. Finns notice length much more than accent.
